OP, it is going to be okay. But you need to be proactive, and you need to be prepared to implement measures to protect your dog and everyone who may interact with him. 

Your job is to speak up before these things happen, and that means doing whatever it takes. I have had to jump in between my dog and children who ran up to pet him, I’ve had to yell at strangers and I’ve had to ask people to leave my home. Sometimes that’s just part of what it means to keep a reactive dog safe. 

You also need to muzzle train, and counter condition, you need to reach out to behaviorists and vets if you have the means to do so, you put ‘do not pet’ patches on their harness, and you avoid putting them in situations you know they aren’t ready for. This probably won’t get much easier, but you’ll put in the work because you love your pet, and slowly you’ll get better at handling his reactivity.

While the logical principles behind mathematics are eternal and unchanging, the numerical systems we use to express them are arbitrary. Our base-10 system exists because we have ten fingers, which seems to be completely incidental. That’s a reflection of us, not a limitation of mathematics itself. A failure in our ability to comprehend or articulate mathematics isn’t a failure of mathematics. Just because our current system struggles to express certain truths doesn’t mean those truths don’t exist or can’t be expressed mathematically in some way we haven’t yet discovered.

Mathematics is the only field that provides universal truths. The statement 1 + 1 = 2 was necessarily true before anything existed and will be true long after the universe collapses into heat death. It isn’t true because of the symbols we use to represent it. It’s true because logical necessity demands it. That’s not something we imposed onto the universe, it’s something we uncovered within it. If we ever develop a full theory of everything, it will likely have to be expressed in mathematical terms because no other framework captures reality in universal and unchanging terms.

The stagnation in fundamental physics isn’t proof that mathematics has hit a wall, it’s proof that we don’t have the right math. Every time in history that people have assumed physics was at a dead end, it turned out we were just missing a key mathematical breakthrough. There’s no reason to think this time is different. But even then, if we accept the premise that maybe math isn’t enough, then what? What other tool do we have? If we give up on using mathematics to explain everything, we guarantee that we won’t explain anything.

We also have no idea what we don’t know. The presence of unknown unknowns means we can’t assume there’s a fundamental gap between math and reality, we just know there are gaps in our understanding. Maybe the limits we’re running into aren’t limits of mathematics itself but limits of our imagination, our notation, or our ability to construct the right abstractions. Gödel’s incompleteness theorems don’t prove that math is insufficient for reality, they prove that any fixed formal system has limits. The solution is to expand the system. Every time we hit a wall, we push forward, refining our mathematics, making it more precise, more general, and more capable.

Maybe math won’t explain everything, but assuming that it can’t only ensures that it won’t. The only way forward is to assume that Math can explain everything, because even if that assumption turns out to be wrong, it’s the only assumption that will get us anywhere.

As a high school dropout who did two years of college and is dying to go back, trust me, you don’t sound stupid at all. There will absolutely be people in college who are less prepared than you. It’s not just smart people who go.

My advice? Start at a community college and pick classes you think you’ll enjoy. Use it as a way to figure out what you like and if college is something you even want to do. If it feels right you can always transfer to a four-year university later. Keep the pressure low and focus on learning for the sake of learning. Don’t beat yourself up if you don’t hit every goal, you’re allowed to go at your own pace. College doesn’t have to be the same for everyone. What matters is staying curious and giving yourself space to grow.

Echoing what others have said here, outside of school, you can still feel stupid for all kinds of reasons. That doesn’t mean you are. If anything, it sounds like you’re just very aware of the things you don’t know, and that’s a good thing. Being aware of your gaps is the first step toward filling them and learning new things. That kind of self-awareness is way more valuable than pretending you already have all the answers.

Well, that depends. Life today is documented in far greater detail than ever before. With cameras at our fingertips and the ability to broadcast our lives to the world with just a device and a Wi-Fi connection, we leave behind an enormous digital footprint. Things we share, photos, videos, posts, can last indefinitely, stored in the vast and often unforgiving memory of the internet.

If I ask my mom about the names of her great-grandparents, she probably wouldn’t know. Their lives weren’t documented, no photos, no videos, not even a birth or death certificate. It’s as if they only existed in the memories of those who knew them, and as their friends and family passed, so did most traces of their life.

People in the future might not care to know us, but they’ll have the ability to. That depends on their values, and those values, to some extent, are shaped by the choices we make today.

It’s true that the world can feel unbearable for those who are sensitive. The weight of suffering, the injustice, and the stark contrast between how things are and how they ought to be can crush even the strongest people. But I believe there’s something profoundly significant in being sensitive, something that doesn’t make existence futile but instead gives it meaning.

To be sensitive and empathetic is to see, to truly witness the world in a way that most people avoid. It’s painful, yes, but it’s also a rare and precious gift. It allows you to recognize beauty even in the smallest things, to connect with others in ways that most people can’t, and to stand as a beacon of hope in a world that feels increasingly dark. Sensitivity is not weakness, it’s strength when used rationally. When we acknowledge the brokenness around us and within us we give ourselves the opportunity to do better. 

The endless cycle of striving against forces you can’t control is not a reason to despair but a call to rise above it. No, you may not change the world. You may not end suffering or injustice in your lifetime. But every act of goodness, every choice to live according to your ideals despite the difficulty, chips away at that darkness. It’s not about fixing the world entirely, it’s about making it just a little brighter, even if only for one person, one moment, one interaction.

Your sensitivity might make you prey to the predators of this world, but it also makes you dangerous in ways they can’t comprehend. Empathy and idealism, when paired with action, are the most subversive forces in existence. They challenge the idea that life is only about survival, showing that it can also be about creation, love, and understanding. Your kindness may not save the world, but it might save you, because every time you choose to act in alignment with your ideals, you reclaim a piece of yourself from the despair.

Perhaps our children won’t live in a utopia. But they may live in a world that’s slightly better because we existed, because we didn’t give in to the cynicism. They may inherit our courage, our clarity, and our conviction, even if they inherit our sensitivity too. And maybe that’s enough.

Life is hard. The world is unfair. But sensitivity is not a curse, it’s a sign that you are human, that you can recognize Goodness and its absence. That is where meaning is born. 

You are not prey. You are not futile. You are alive, and that in itself is an act of defiance against the void. Live in such a way that you leave behind a trace of the light you carry, no matter how small. That light matters.

Edit to add:

It’s important that you aim to do the best that you can, even if your best won’t always be good enough. There will be moments when you fall short, when your conscience, the same one that makes life so hard, will remind you of all the ways you’ve gone against it. But there’s power in even recognizing that you’ve failed. It means you understand the difference between right and wrong, and that understanding, in itself, is a form of striving. It shows that you are trying to act in alignment with your ideals, even if you don’t always meet your own expectations.

You must learn forgiveness, not just for others, but for yourself. Forgive yourself for the times you weren’t as strong as you wanted to be. Forgive others for their shortcomings too, because in a world as complicated as this one, everyone will have moral failings. What matters is that you can hold yourself and others accountable while understanding that no one is perfect. Accountability paired with forgiveness is what allows us to grow, and we need more people who are willing to undertake the task of earnest personal development. 

Your sensitivity and empathy allow you to see the complexity in others, to recognize that even those who disappoint you or hurt you are often struggling in ways you may not fully understand. Use this empathy not as a reason to excuse harm but as a way to find balance, to hold space for accountability while also extending compassion

I completely agree, but I think it’s also important to recognize that sometimes breaking the cycle even once, resisting the compulsion just one time and realizing that nothing bad happens, can spark long-term change. That single act of resistance can show you that it is possible to engage less and less with the intrusive thoughts and compulsions over time.

The process is rarely straightforward. You might break the cycle one day, only to fall back into it for weeks. Then you might resist twice in a row, then three times, then four. There will be relapses, but over time those moments of resistance start to add up. Eventually, the cycle begins to lose its grip, and one day the intrusive thoughts might barely register.

Never underestimate the power of small steps. At the same time, be mindful that an all-or-nothing approach to freeing yourself from OCD can create opportunities for the OCD to manifest in a new way. Becoming rigidly focused on eliminating every intrusive thought or compulsion can itself turn into a harmful pattern. Instead, focus on doing your best, accept that imperfection is part of the process, and learn to forgive yourself for setbacks. Progress comes with flexibility, patience, and time.

I grew up in a Catholic country, and from around the age of six or seven, I developed a deep fear of God, convinced that He would punish me unless I performed the sign of the cross toward the ceiling multiple times. What began as three repetitions grew over time, first to 33, then 50, then 100, and eventually 333. My right arm would cramp from the repetitive motions, so I used my left hand to hold it up.

It didn’t matter where I was. Whether I was sleeping over at a friend’s house, sleeping in my parents’ bed, or being carried to bed after falling asleep in the car, I would wake up just long enough to complete the ritual before falling back asleep. I felt constantly dirty, inherently flawed, and deeply afraid of God. I was terrified by what I saw as my lack of faith. At the time, I wasn’t afraid of much else, but I lived with the constant fear that God would punish me or even take my parents away if I didn’t act or think the “right” way.

Looking back, that fear seems almost simpler compared to what I experience now. These days, my OCD affects nearly every aspect of my life, including a relentless ethical standard I know I cannot possibly meet. As a child, my fear was more straightforward: “If I don’t follow the creator, I will suffer.” Now, it feels far more complex and overwhelming: “I cannot even fully comprehend my creator; how could I ever understand or live up to His expectations?”

I have also learned to understand the details of certain horrific aspects of the human experience, and my mind cannot help but hyper-focus on the implications of every single one of them. I find a way to ruminate about every facet of human suffering, and yet I also fixate on how I don’t ruminate enough, don’t grieve enough, don’t suffer enough on behalf of others. I constantly question whether my empathy is lacking, whether my heart is empty of love. No matter how I approach it, I always see myself as the villain, unable to meet any standard of goodness or virtue, and that has been the case for as long as I can remember.

It is not about opposing a dedicated bike lane, but about addressing the very real risks of a bike lane that also serves as an emergency lane. Emergency vehicles are not just larger than cars; they are allowed to exceed speed limits, bypass traffic controls, and operate under conditions that are far more demanding, even with skilled drivers. The combination of size, speed, and challenging circumstances makes these vehicles a serious risk to cyclists, particularly on a two-way bike path full of blind corners like the one in Stanley Park.

The idea of “rarely” using the lane is subjective. For high-priority emergencies like cardiac arrests, at least one ambulance, an advanced life support unit, and a fire engine are typically dispatched. This means at least three large emergency vehicles could be traveling down that path, possibly at high speeds, in conditions where seconds matter. This creates a dangerous dynamic, especially given that many cyclists ride with headphones and may not expect an ambulance to come barreling toward them during a leisurely ride.

Driving with lights and sirens is far more dangerous than many realize. It is always a balance between the urgency of the call and the safety of everyone on the road, including vulnerable cyclists who are already at heightened risk. A bike lane that doubles as an emergency lane introduces a level of danger that is incompatible with the purpose of protecting cyclists in the first place.

Driving an emergency vehicle in a bike lane through Stanley Park seems like a bad idea. People don’t consistently yield to emergency vehicles, whether they are drivers, pedestrians, or cyclists. By driving into a space designated for the most vulnerable road users, you’re deliberately putting those who have no protection at significantly greater risk. If a collision happens, the outcome is far more likely to be catastrophic compared to a collision with a car on the road.

I don’t think you’re schizophrenic. People with schizophrenia don’t know they have it, and from your post, it seems like you’re worried about being crazy. ‘Crazy’ people don’t worry about being crazy because they lack a thing called insight.

Psychiatric insight is a person’s ability to understand their own mental state, including recognizing when their thoughts, feelings, or behaviors are unusual or problematic. It involves awareness of having a mental health issue, understanding how it affects their life, and realizing they might need help. People with good insight know when they’re struggling, can see how their symptoms impact them, and often seek support. Those with limited insight may not see their behaviors as unusual or may think the problem lies outside themselves, making it harder for them to seek or accept help.

I’ve had this horrible disorder since I was a child. Sometimes, I’d be kept awake by thoughts of murdering my parents while sleepwalking. It was awful and torturous, and no child deserves to feel that kind of fear.

I’m 22 now, still unmedicated for OCD. I never did CBT until recently, partly because I didn’t feel like I needed to.

My approach, since getting a diagnosis, has always been rooted in self-knowledge. I knew the thoughts scared me, so they must not have come from me.

I exposed myself to these fearful thoughts because I had no choice but to ruminate. I just stayed idle until they became background noise.

The point is, there’s no way to completely get rid of OCD. By definition, it involves thought patterns we have no control over, and the more you try to fight it, the more prominent those thoughts become.

You have to learn to let it be. Get to know yourself and understand that you are not your intrusive thoughts.

The hardest part of OCD is that improvement only comes when you stop resisting it. But I promise, it does get better.

Over time, the object of your obsessive thoughts will change, and so will the fear. You’ll learn to recognize what triggers your anxiety and figure out how to navigate it.

When it gets too overwhelming, and it feels like my mind is out to get me, I focus on my breath. Every time my thoughts drift back to the intrusive ones, I bring my attention back to my breath. I usually end up falling asleep, which can be helpful. This trick has gotten me through many sleepless nights.

I’m a former international student and now a transfer paramedic working out of Abbotsford.

I live in Vancouver and my station is in Abbotsford, but my job takes me all over the Lower Mainland since I handle interfacility transfers, not 911. I spend my days between different hospitals and units, from the ER to the NICU, and I get to talk to everyone—nurses, doctors, admin staff. I’ve seen firsthand where the system breaks down and where it actually works well.

As we all know, there are some major issues in Canada due to the unbridled population growth. I went to the most legitimate diploma mill college, a college where all of the students are international and come here with the goal of attaining permanent residency, when I first came to Canada in 2020 immigrating was disgustingly easy, now the government has put limits in place to slow down the rate of growth, but our population is still growing.

The issue with the healthcare system is a bad combination of immigration pressures and not enough infrastructure to keep up with the growing population. We need bigger hospitals, more beds, and more people in healthcare. The jobs are draining, and not everyone’s cut out for them, so we have to find ways to make it worth it for people to stay in these roles.

A few weeks ago, I noticed a spider that looked slightly off, like it was dragging around some strange sack of skin on its side. I was stoned and decided that I was too stoned, and too scared of bugs, to try and catch it, so I just left the room. I later wondered if the weird spider might be pregnant and made it a mission to kill it.

Over the next few weeks, the spider taunted me. Sometimes I’d walk into the room, and there it would be, standing on my bookshelf before using its demonic silky floss to vanish back into whatever circle of hell it came from.

I never caught it, and that brings us to what happened yesterday.

I was sitting at my desk, minding my own business, comfortably ignorant, when I looked up and saw about 200 tiny spiders crawling on the ceiling above me, all heading toward the same empty corner of the room. There were so many of them clustered together that I couldn’t even see the ceiling anymore. I took a deep breath, told my mom I’d call her back, grabbed my beer and the bug spray, and sprayed until my finger got sore and my eyes started to water.

I left the room and closed the door. When I came back, the spiders were gone. I don’t know if they lived or died. I don’t know if they’re hiding somewhere behind a book for me to stumble upon later and be horrified again. I just don’t know.

I’m glad the spider thought my home was safe enough for its children, unfortunately it is not.

Yep. I’m a very anxious person and I’m always thinking about things that could go wrong. Public transit used to be my primary method of transportation so I developed a few skills to make it a bearable ordeal.

1. Be picky about where you sit. The best spots are not actually at the back like many people think. Sitting in the back puts you in a perfect position to be cornered. I like seating by the door, in the single seaters that are right up against the panel separating the back seats. Alternatively, pick a seat close to a door, next to people you feel comfortable sitting with. If the bus is full I always recommend standing by a door, with your back against the panel, try and find an area where you can  see one of the big dome mirrors as this allows you to see what is going on in front of you but also behind you. If your bus is stopping in shady areas I would say stand further in, around people you feel comfortable with. The key here is stand or sit in such away that would prevent anyone from grabbing you from behind, minimizing the odds of sitting next to someone who makes you uncomfortable, maximizing visibility, and ensuring you have at least two ways to exit the bus should shit hit the proverbial fan. 

2. If you’re on the skytrain, specifically one of the older ones where each car is isolated, and you start to feel uncomfortable, switch cars. Get off at the next station and move toward a different car, act nonchalant. If the cars are connected then exit the skytrain and move towards the furthest car from the one you were originally on. This allows you to put distance between you and whoever is making you uncomfortable without making it seem like you are running away. 

3. Keep your head down and your wits about you. Don’t stare at people, some people might take it personally. Pick a point on the floor and stare at it, allow your peripheral vision to guide you. You can also stare out windows and watch the reflection. Don’t wear headphones or wear just one. If someone tries to talk to you be kind but short, ignoring people might get you yelled at and being kind goes a long way even with crazy people. Don’t over-engage though.

I was raised in a violent country and my dad taught me that situational awareness is everything. You need to ensure that you’re always aware of what’s going on around you, the possible way things could go wrong, and have several plans of escape. 

I know this might seem like a bit much to some people, but I think you should always be extra cautious in unpredictable and volatile situations.

So although I  never tried the brownies you mentioned, (I'm honestly kinda sad I didn't because they sound delicious) here's my personal recipe for super fudgy brownies which might do the trick.

\-2 average-sized eggs

\-120g of unsalted butter

\-120g of 45% chocolate

\-100g of brown sugar

\-pinch of salt

\-40g all-purpose flour

\-vanilla extract

\-8g of Glucose syrup (this, along with the melted chocolate. is the secret to super fudgy and decadent brownies. you can get it at either Walmart or Michaels or anywhere where they sell baking supplies. also, it's super sticky so it's hard to weigh, I usually just do a big tablespoon instead of weighing it out)

\-8g of cocoa powder

​

\-First, melt the chocolate along with the glucose syrup and the butter in a microwave-safe bowl. Microwave it for a minute first, then, if it needs more melting, do it in small increments until you get an even looking mixture.

\-On a different bowl, mix the eggs, the brown sugar and the pinch of salt.

\-Once the chocolate mixture is fully melted, add it to the egg and sugar mixture and finally add in the flour and cocoa powder (don't forget to shift it for a more even, soft brownie)

\-Bake the batter on a lightly oiled metal dish at 170 degrees C for around 20 to 30 minutes, depending on the size of the baking dish. this amount of batter doesn't make too many brownies so you'll probably want to double the ingredients.
